utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Edgerton, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Jahic into the courtroom. Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. While the witness is being brought in, to indicate that I received via email at 6.00 yesterday evening a intercept witness authentication receipt. This is rather late, but leaving that aside, I had a quick word with Ms. Edgerton prior to Your Honours coming on the Bench, and apparently Ms. Edgerton does not propose to tender this particular document, but to deal with, I think, three of the conversations via viva voce questioning. So there -- I guess there are basically two points. First of all, Your Honour, it's not acceptable to have this sort of material served so late. And I place a marker there to avoid future occurrences of this nature. I appreciate that Ms. Edgerton is doing her best with the time she has available, but that's what we have to do as well, Your Honour. And it places additional strain on the Defence. Now -- and the second point is, of course, that, Your Honour, I would be objecting to analyses of conversation based on the sort of conjecture and speculation that's contained within the sort of comments that are made on these, in relation to these intercepts. So I'm just placing that on the record now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you would be objecting to analyses of conversation based on the -- yes. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour's aware of the sort of document we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But we haven't seen it in relation to this witness. So whether there's any conjecture or speculation, we do not know. But at least you consider it to be speculative and --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we'll deal with it at the time, Your Honour, after the witness has heard the intercepts in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you noticed the marker made by Ms. Loukas, and of course the conjecture and speculation, of course, Ms. Loukas, we know what to expect from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we -- of course we can't rule on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not in advance. I'm just placing a marker there so Your Honours are aware of it and we can deal with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and not be surprised at that moment when it comes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please escort Mr. Jahic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Edgerton: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, to begin with this morning I would just like to ask you three brief questions in relation to the testimony you gave to the Trial Chamber yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the information of the Trial Chamber, the first question rises at page 9 of yesterday's transcript beginning at line number 2. Mr. Jahic, yesterday you told us that Stup was to the north of Ahatovici because there's Bojnik, and it's at the entrance to the city of Sarajevo itself. And I wonder in light of that, when you answered that first question, you didn't have the map that you now have beside you available. Could you just turn to that map and see if you can locate the place known as Stup on that map.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before doing that, I would maybe like to make a correction. My answer at the time was a bit hasty. Perhaps Stup is not where I said it was. Thinking back, I now think it's south of Ahatovici. I may have been wrong before. But I can show it on the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could quickly do that.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stup is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I believe the witness is indicating a location south of the settlement of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think now, that having been done, we could remove the map to allow the interpreters to better see the witness as he's continuing to speak. Now, just to move on to the second question. Mr. Jahic, yesterday at page 51 of the transcript of yesterday's testimony, but in any case yesterday, you identified a friend of yours by the name of Armin Mujkic who told you that a man who threw some kind of gas bomb into the cistern was a former chauffeur or bodyguard for Krajisnik and Jovo Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, the transcript at page 51 indicates it was a friend of mine, very close friend of mine, et cetera, et cetera. And I think that Ms. Edgerton said chauffeur or bodyguard. The actual evidence is chauffeur and bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Chauffeur and bodyguard. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, did your friend identify this person by any kind of name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall with any certainty or precision now. I just remember that he was very certain about the identity of that person because this friend of mine had been in the reserve police force, in the police administration of Novi Grad, and it was his job to guard the house of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page of the transcript, page 51, Mr. Jahic, you mentioned there was one occasion when this SRNA television from Pale arrived, and then further down you say "we received a piece of paper with a text that we were supposed to reproduce before the TV cameras." Going on to page 52 of the transcript. Mr. Jahic, at this time, do you recall what the paper read, what you were told to say?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the text was to the effect that there was a large concentration of the Green Beret, mujahedin, HOS forces, foreign mercenaries in Ahatovici, that they were paid a lot of money, that we were mercenaries ourselves, that the conditions in the camp were very good indeed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, Your Honour, I'll be moving to the intercepted communications at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have now, Mr. Jahic, three intercepted telephone communications that I'd like you to listen to in succession.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I should note, we'll be seeking to play the audios of these communications in their entirety. None of these intercepted communications -- none of the audios for these communications have previously been tendered, but one of them has had its transcript marked as Exhibit P282. That would be the one which on your list, Your Honour, is incorrectly noted as the 5th of June. It should read the 8th of June -- sorry, the 15th of June 1992. Now, Your Honour, just in terms of marking the audios and transcripts, those three intercepts are being -- with the related transcripts prepared on one CD for the Trial Chamber, which is being provided in short order. I would be looking in part for Your Honours' direction, but what I would propose to do is to mark that CD with the audios and related transcripts as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then withdraw 282 -- yes, 282, or?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There lies the problem, Your Honour. 282 was the number of a transcript that was shown to a previous witness, protected witness 623. So I think we have to leave 282 in place, and give these now a further new number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it should be avoided that we give the same exhibits under different numbers, you're allowed to proceed as you suggested. So we have -- the 282 transcript now also appears in the new bundle, both audio and on paper which then has number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The audio will be Prosecution Exhibit P369. The transcript of 30 May 1992 will be P369A. The transcript from 08/06/1992 will be P369B. And the transcript of 15 June 1992 will be P369C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the translation will then have the .1 numbers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And further, Your Honour, we're providing the Trial Chamber and the witness today with highlighted copies of those transcripts because what I'd like to do is play them, and then direct the witness back to particular portions of the transcript. So this is only by way of ease of reference for the people in Court today. And we'll begin when everyone has received their copies with the intercept of 30 May 1992. If we could begin then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, I'd like you to listen closely to this intercepted communication. And if it helps you to follow along with the transcript you've just received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid any defective transcripts, the English audio should be translated into French. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unidentified female: Hello. Unidentified male: Hello. Unidentified female: How can I help you? Yes. Good evening. Unidentified male: Good evening. 657848. It's the government, Belgrade. Unidentified female: Excuse me? Unidentified male: It's the government, Belgrade. Unidentified female: Excuse me? Unidentified male: Government, Belgrade. Unidentified female: What can I do for you? Unidentified male: 657848. Unidentified female: Hold on a moment, please. Unidentified male: Hello. Unidentified female: Hello. Unidentified male: Hello. Unidentified female: Yes. Good evening. Unidentified male: Good evening. 657848. ... Government. Belgrade, here. Is Mico there? Unidentified female: No, Mico's not in. No, he's not. He's on a business trip. Let me tell you -- Just hold on, please. Hello. Unidentified male: Yes. Unidentified female: Lale? Hold on, please. You probably need to speak with the other Mico, right? Hold on, please. Cedo: Hello. Lale: Hello. This is Lale here. Cedo: This is Cedo. What can I do for you? Lale: Yes. Cedo: Well, momentarily he's up there on the hill, you know. 783. Hold on. If you need the phone number, I'll give it to you. Just hold on a second. Hello. Lale? Do you want to speak to Davidovic? Mico Davidovic? Our Mico. All right. Hold on, please. Lale: Hello? Cedo: Look, it's 800 020. That's it. Lale: I'll put on a man who wants to talk to you a little. Cedo: All right. Radovan Karadzic: Hello. Cedo: Good evening. Radovan Karadzic: How are you? Cedo: Fine. Who is it? Radovan Karadzic: It's Radovan. Have there been any attacks tonight? Cedo: Yes, there have been some in Rajlovac. The attack has been repelled. Now there's a buildup of troops here near the shopping centre. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Cedo: The Green Berets are assembling there, and there's a huge buildup. We're expecting an attack on Vrace. Radovan Karadzic: Vrace? Cedo: Yes. Radovan Karadzic: Uh-huh. Cedo: Nothing else? Radovan Karadzic: No artillery? Cedo: No, no artillery on either side. Radovan Karadzic: All right. Cedo: Are you fine? Radovan Karadzic: Yes. Try not to use artillery. Has Mladic called? Cedo: Yes, yes, we've arranged that. Radovan Karadzic: Tell them to go to hell -- Cedo: Exactly. Radovan Karadzic: If they want to die... Cedo: All right. Radovan Karadzic: Could you remind Mico to urgently send the papers for that man up there, to Devedlaka. Cedo: Yes, yes. I understand, I understand. To appoint Dragan. Radovan Karadzic: It is urgent, and it has to be done. There are many things that don't function here. Cedo: Well, yes, but we also have other information. Radovan Karadzic: I don't know what's going on. Cedo: I have completely different information. That's why I don't understand... I'm afraid this isn't about one dimension because the official authorities are -- Yes, but there is other information, too. We'll tell you. Anyway, there are no problems. If there is any, I'll tell the minister. Radovan Karadzic: Let's put him on now. Cedo: It's not about an unimportant person after all. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Cedo: If it had been about a small mayor who we wanted replaced, but it's not. So we have some basis. Radovan Karadzic: If you agree, you should then invite this guy up to Pale. Cedo: Yes, and then you can have some talk in peace. Radovan Karadzic: Zugic's like an indicator here. I think Zugic's right. Cedo: Yeah, possible. It's possible he's right, but if you agree -- I don't want to make a hasty decision here. And as a consequence, the commission would visit, right? Radovan Karadzic: We'll have the people up there who are to take care of it. Cedo: Exactly. I think that would be the best thing to do. We just talked and exchanged opinions. We also have other information regarding that. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Cedo: You know how it is. The question has always been there, "What if we don't succeed?" Radovan Karadzic: I restrained myself from exaggerating because it's easy to make a mistake. Cedo: That's what I'm afraid of. I'll tell the minister about your suggestion. I'll call you back sometime. Radovan Karadzic: Take care of that quickly. Cedo: Yes, sure. Radovan Karadzic: Is everything under control? Cedo: Well, half of Dobrinje is under our control, and the other half is under their control. Radovan Karadzic: They're not attacking the airport today? Cedo: Well, they haven't. Radovan Karadzic: Did they shell Lukavica yesterday? Cedo: Hell, yes. Oh, yeah. Radovan Karadzic: They set on fire some cars there, right? Cedo: Well, yeah. They set on fire whatever cars there were there. Yes, they shelled. They, too, have artillery. They point one part of it at us, and with the other they provoke themselves. Radovan Karadzic: Yeah. Cedo: So... Radovan Karadzic: Yes, all right. Here all Serb artillery shall be silent, and everything that is heard will be theirs. Cedo: Exactly, sure. Radovan Karadzic: Cedo, tell everyone there I said hello. Cedo: Cheers, have a good one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, you've clearly heard now the conversation which has just been played to you. I'd like to direct your attention, then, to the portion that appears at the bottom of page 3 of your transcript, and for the Trial Chamber, the same excerpt appears at the top of page 3 of the English language transcript. And I quote: "Radovan Karadzic: I'm all right. Have there been any attacks tonight? Cedo: Yes, there have been some in Rajlovac. Radovan Karadzic: In Rajlovac? Cedo: They went for that barracks there from Ahatovici, and that attack has been repelled. Now there's a buildup of troops here near the shopping centre." Mr. Jahic, I know the date of this conversation is 30 May 1992. I understand from your testimony yesterday that you were in Ahatovici on 30 May 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, on that date, were there any attacks from Ahatovici to any barracks, Rajlovac or any other JNA facilities in the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There were no attacks. And for the reason -- the reason why is that there were a hundred of us, to 120. We were poorly armed. It would have been complete nonsense to do that with that number of men and that equipment, to attack a military facility such as the barracks at Butile and Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on to the next conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I note that appears on Your Honours' list as a conversation dated 5 June 1992 which is incorrect. The date of the conversation is 8 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Milena: Hello Rajlovac? Mijatovic: Yes. Milena: Just a moment. President Krajisnik would like to talk to somebody. Mijatovic: Thank you. Rajka, is that you? Milena: Who's that? Mijatovic: Mijatovic is here. Rajka, is that you? Milena: Milena here. Well, Milena, Mijatovic is here. Milena: Just a moment please. Mijatovic: Thank you. Momcilo Krajisnik: Hello. Mijatovic: Hello. Momcilo Krajisnik: Hello, Mato, Kum. Mijatovic: Hello, how are you? Momcilo Krajisnik: What are you doing? Well, even if you know them or don't know them, they're all brothers. We're as men from Herzegovina, all the best men in power. What's new? Mijatovic: That Momcilo Moro was killed yesterday. Well, yesterday in front of the shells at the depot. Momcilo Krajisnik: Is Ljubisa Vladisic there? Mirko told me there were problems with those prisoners and the other stuff. Mijatovic: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: If you find a solution, it's okay. If you don't find a solution, you can include us, then I will come for consultation. We shall not do anything wrong, you know. Mijatovic: Well, okay. Momcilo Krajisnik: You know that one, khoja, it is an occasion now. Khoja, she's young. Mijatovic: I know, I know. Momcilo Krajisnik: We should not do anything that is, well, something that is not characteristic for the Serbian people. Dishonesty never leads to anything good, you know. Mijatovic: I agree. Momcilo Krajisnik: But we should do -- not do anything, anything that does not follow the rules. Isn't that so? Mijatovic: I know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Because they have released some men. They went from here. They're back again. Mijatovic: Well, I think, with these women, they're accommodated, I think, as many as it was possible, women, children, and old men, to be under those conditions. And the military part is for the military police, and that part will be processed and so on. They're investigating interviewing, complete it. Now, what they're going to do, I don't know. Momcilo Krajisnik: But let me tell you, I'm just suggesting that you do that. It should be something that is characteristic, typical of the Serbian people. Mijatovic: That's true. Momcilo Krajisnik: Of course, normally. Okay, send my regards to everyone. Mijatovic: And tomorrow they said at 10.00, the meeting with you. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Mijatovic: Up there. Momcilo Krajisnik: And we'll agree. Mijatovic: All right. Ljubisa. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay. Well, thank God that you're -- Ljubisa Vladusic: Yes, that's always been your thesis, in the first sentence, whenever we met. Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, I'm just joking. You know that I have to attack just a bit, and then others will attack me. Yes, how's your mother and others back home? Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, to be honest, not very well. Momcilo Krajisnik: What's wrong with her? Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, you know, she has angina pectoris and so on, so if anything happens, her blood pressure rises, her health worsens, but what can I do? Yes, and how are you? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, I'm okay, not bad. Ljubisa Vladusic: How are you coping? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, what can I do? Thank God, you know how it is to handle people's work with lots of problems. Ljubisa Vladusic: What can we do? Momcilo Krajisnik: What can we do? Well, to win if it's God's will. Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, let's hope so. Momcilo Krajisnik: Do you have your doubts? Ljubisa Vladusic: No, I don't have doubts. If I had all the information, I'd probably think the same as you. But as I've just a slight idea about some things, then I have to ask you. I hope you don't mind my asking. Momcilo Krajisnik: No, no. Don't worry. Ljubisa Vladusic: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: Trust me. Ljubisa Vladusic: I trust you. Well, if I don't trust you -- Momcilo Krajisnik: No, I'm telling them now. Ljubisa Vladusic: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: No, nothing should be done towards people. It is not characteristic of real men, and not characteristic for the Serbian people. Ljubisa Vladusic: That's true. Momcilo Krajisnik: There's no one that should -- innocent people such as the Muslims are, and someone put arms in their hands -- if they didn't do anything, if they didn't just surrender. Well, that Gacanovic, of course, you know what -- Ljubisa Vladusic: Wait a minute. Do you have any influence on that? Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes, I do, and I have told that to the soldiers. No one could do anything. They're now implementing, you understand. No one can do anything that's wrong. Ljubisa Vladusic: I was just talking with Mirko about that, and I'm glad that he's the same opinion as you are. He thinks exactly the same. I'm glad because of that. And I think that many things are involved. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay. Ljubisa Vladusic: It would be a shame, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: No, there's no doubt there. One cannot engage in genocide to achieve anything. I know that it is difficult when someone's killed. Ljubisa Vladusic: Quiet, quiet. I had a conflict because of it. Okay, it's turned out all right, but I was just joking with your best man. Momcilo Krajisnik: Which one? Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, Joja. We're sitting up there, and he came and attacked me and said why -- I expressed my condolences publicly in the newspaper. Momcilo Krajisnik: About whom? Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, the guy -- the young guy that was killed in front of the barracks. You remember that, Secerovic, the one from the SDP party, that one. Momcilo Krajisnik: You shouldn't have done it, you know. Ljubisa Vladusic: No, no, Momo. We were very good friends for many years. Momcilo Krajisnik: Now look -- Ljubisa Vladusic: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: This is not the time for that. The problem was because it was in public. A few days ago, they skinned a man here in Hrasnica. But the policy should be waged according to the people. Politics should be managed as is characteristic of those people, not of these monsters. Ljubisa Vladusic: All right. Momcilo Krajisnik: How are you? Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, I've -- I called you several times, and Rajka, too, and so I conveyed something to Mirko. But you know about the information flow. It's enough that you're late just one hour, and it's not current any longer. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Ljubisa Vladusic: On the other hand, as you know, I was in town for long time, and I was able to communicate with those men. You know the two that I'm talking about. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. And what happened? Well, simply what the hell happened to them? Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, I don't know. They tried to meet you. I don't know if Mirko passed all this on to you because I tried to reach you several times. Momcilo Krajisnik: And we talked, and he said -- Ljubisa Vladusic: No, no. Your Mirko. Did he pass everything on to you? Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes, he did. I tried to reach them. We called from here. Ljubisa Vladusic: It's like this. I talked to him this morning and they'll call you. Momcilo Krajisnik: Who? Ljubisa Vladusic: The two of them. Momcilo Krajisnik: But listen. Why did they need to do that? I know what they're thinking of. Ljubisa Vladusic: Momo, I can't explain this to you over the phone. Politics or diplomacy can play a role. Politics is a bitch. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes, well, that's what I'm saying. Ljubisa Vladusic: I'd like to suggest something. Of course, if I can make a suggestion to you, I would suggest that it would be a good idea because they're asking for your initiative to sit down and meet with them any way you decide. Momcilo Krajisnik: You know it's very dangerous for me to sit down and negotiate with them because they'll declared -- well, I don't know. I'd like to help them. I have a good opinion of them. I mean, a good opinion. As far as diplomacy and all of that stuff is concerned, I don't think they're traitors, but they have messed it up so badly for themselves I don't know how to sort things out. Ljubisa Vladusic: Why wouldn't -- shouldn't they be mediators as regards solving these problems? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, I can't tell you that over the phone. Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, neither can I. I've talked to them on many issues, and I can't tell you all that over the phone now. That's why I thought that if you could set aside five minutes for me to explain things to you. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay, well, we'll sit down together. Ljubisa Vladusic: Momo, we can have an agreement. Well, I don't know if there's enough room for me to come with him. Momcilo Krajisnik: Who with? Ljubisa Vladusic: With Momo. Well, let me say there are a couple of things that I'd like to tell you. And of course -- Momcilo Krajisnik: You talk to them first, and then you can tell them what I think. Ljubisa Vladusic: Well, I talked to them yesterday, talk to them every day. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right, fine. But come tomorrow. Ljubisa Vladusic: All right, fine. Momcilo Krajisnik: Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, you've clearly heard and understood everything in this last conversation you've just listened to?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention then to page 2 of the transcript you're reviewing, and the relevant portion also appears near the top of page 2 of the English language version of the transcript. And I quote: "Krajisnik, Momcilo: Because they've released some men, they went from here, they're back again, and yes, yes, so they're attacking, aren't they? Mijatovic: Yes, that's it. Krajisnik, Momcilo: Well, you see it you're a smart man. So that -- Mijatovic: You know what? Why is this part now to say so separated, military and civilian. Krajisnik, Momcilo: Yes. Mijatovic: Well, here I think we these women they are accommodated I think, as many as it was possible, women, children, and old men, with certain conditions. And the military part, that is for the military police, and that part there will be processed and so on. They're investigating, completing it, and now what they are going to process, believe me that, that, I don't know." Mr. Jahic, referring to the phrase "because they've released some men, they went from here, they're back again. Yes, yes, so they're attacking, aren't they," do you know who these men are the participants in this conversation are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I foreshadowed, this is a matter I would be objecting to. There has been no foundation established for the witness to be asked to proffer an opinion in relation to this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first ask the parties whether this is a matter we could discuss in the presence of the witness or whether we should rather discuss it in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would have thought it's a matter that must be discussed in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, may I ask you to leave the courtroom for a moment. We have a procedural matter to discuss before you answer that question, if at all. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Jahic out of the courtroom. Ms. Edgerton, you heard the objection by Ms. Loukas. Would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a matter of weight, in fact. And I think it's at the Court's discretion having heard the intercept in its entirety and having heard the evidence of the witness in this case to decide what weight they're going to give what comment he has to make about the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Finally, it's always the -- if evidence is admitted, then of course it's always up to the Chamber to assess the weight of that evidence. What leads you to believe that this conversation is about something the witness could testify about?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are -- there's other factors mentioned in this conversation, including the personalities and the interlocutors of Mr. Krajisnik that lead the Prosecution to believe that the conversation is about a situation the witness knows about. For example, and linking this to the witness's testimony, there's mention in the conversation later on of one Gacanovic family. The witness has already spoken in his testimony yesterday about people with the surname Gacanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, because it went very quickly, guide us to the...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The English language transcript, that appears on page 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He has also Your Honour, yesterday, spoken about the men who he has been detained with in the cisterns and where they came from. He has described a number of men from Bratunac who told him they had come to end up in his village from Bratunac, after having been detained in Pale, exchanged in Visoko. And then to Ahatovici. And it's our position, Your Honour, that based on that evidence yesterday, the witness is able to comment on the portion I've just asked him about, that being: "They've released some men. They went from here. They're back again."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to find the -- yesterday's testimony about Gacanovic. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 21, Your Honour, of yesterday's transcript, lines 9 and 10. He mentions one Avdo Gacanovic as one of the people who were killed in their initial efforts to escape from the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, Ms. Edgerton draws our attention, I would say, specifically to the name Gacanovic appearing, and the other one is the names of the -- of those who are speaking. Ms. Edgerton, may I first ask you: What's specific about those names apart from that one of the names is, of course, that of the accused. But, as such, that would not make the witness aware of the events, is it, that are discussed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Prosecution -- it's going to be the Prosecution's argument that these other participants in the conversation are in one case a political figure in Novi Grad Municipality; in another case, someone who was otherwise close to Mr. Krajisnik and the Bosnian Serb leadership. But that doesn't necessarily mean, Your Honour, that these are people who the witness has any knowledge of or acquaintance with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- I think you're now talking about Vladusic to be a political figure in --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was in that regard referring to Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Vladusic, an acquaintance of Mr. Krajisnik at the very least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not talking about the last transcript, but about this one. So you draw our attention, as you say there are some features in this conversation, one of them being, let's say, not locals who then are discussed. And that would be congruent with what the witness testified yesterday. And the second point is the name of Gacanovic which appeared in his testimony yesterday, and also appears here, and for that reason we could accept that this witness might be able to link this conversation to what he experienced? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's our submission he is in a position to do that, Your Honour. And in any case, were he not present, the Prosecution would be making the same argument in due course about this intercept, taking into account the other evidence about the witness -- about which the witness might not be aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The two basic points appear to be that this name, Gacanovic, is mentioned. Well, that would be fine if there was only one person called Gacanovic in the entirety of Bosnia. That's the first point, Your Honour. In relation to the indication of this person Mijatovic, well, Your Honour, there has been no evidence thus far of any indication that this person is in any way connected with the Municipality of Novi Grad. Thirdly, Your Honour, in relation to this question of -- well, in any event, the Prosecution would be making submissions, my submission in relation to that, Your Honour, is, of course, that's entirely appropriate, the whole -- generally, the question of analysis and the inferences that are to be garnered from examining the intercepts is something for the Trial Chamber. And unless a proper foundation has been laid by the Prosecution, questioning of a witness without a proper foundation is entirely inappropriate when the intercepts just as a document may speak for themselves and the Trial Chamber can make a determination on the evidence and the inferences that are available on the evidence. But to introduce evidence of this nature on this, I would submit, rather flimsy basis, Your Honour, is in my submission not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the complains is that Mr. Mijatovic has not been introduced as -- in the capacity you've described him. Is it your point that that's already in evidence, or will you present any evidence on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not through this witness, Your Honour, but it is the Prosecution's intention to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the first matter. And the second one is that: What could the witness add to this intercept apart from the text as it is? But perhaps first I ask: Ms. Loukas, would there be any objection by the Defence that this -- if this intercept would be admitted into evidence without any further link to a witness, or perhaps just by a witness who could that say he received this intercept from certain persons, that it was intercepted at a certain date? I mean, would you accept, would the Defence accept this intercept to be admitted into evidence solely on the basis of where it comes from?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course the question of intercepts is a quite separate question in relation to -- there's still issues ultimately that we'll be addressing in relation to intercepts. But the intercepts per se, as it stands, no, Your Honour, there would be no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Ms. Edgerton, what are you intending to ask the witness that could add something to the intercept as such?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the first question, I'm intending to ask the witness if he knows who these men who were released and came back to fight might be, especially given he has referred to that in his previous testimony. With respect to the second question, that's about the name Gacanovic. And I stand to be corrected, but, well, it's not clear in the English language version of this transcript. In the B/C/S version, I'm given to understand that when reference is made to Gacanovic, it's made in the plural, referring to the family rather than to an individual. And it's my intention to ask the witness with reference to the name Gacanovic whether or not he could identify, if he knows who they are referring to or what they're referring to, and whether or not the family name Gacanovic was a common name in the settlement of Ahatovici, whether or not Gacanovic was a large or significant family.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour, and not to belabour the point, but I think whether the mention of Gacanovic is in the single or in the plural, the point still stands. There is not just one person called Gacanovic in Bosnia. One assumes, and there has been no evidence to the contrary, nor just one family. So it's a tenuous causal link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on how widespread the name Gacanovic is in the whole of the territory and in that specific territory. Let me just confer for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the basis for asking this witness questions about what appears on -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The questions you had in mind for the witness in relation to what appears on page 1 and page 2 as highlighted, that is where mention is made about some men that had been released and that they went from there and that they are back again is not solid enough. That's not a solid enough basis to ask the witness to find out whether these are the same men as he mentioned yesterday. That would easily come to speculation which will not assist the Chamber. On the other hand, the portion on page 4 of the transcript where the Gacanovic name is mentioned, the Chamber allows you to ask questions about whether he can identify anything that would link this conversation to his testimony of yesterday, and I take it that you have noticed that Ms. Loukas said that Gacanovic was a quite common name, as far as I understand, in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that of course, if you would please explore that in more detail, then the Chamber finally will be better able to assess the relevance of this telephone intercept for any determinations it will have to make. That's one. And if you say that the English does not properly reflect the plural which appears in the original, then you're invited to ask the interpreters to listen to that portion or to read the B/C/S version and to explain to the Chamber whether the reference is to a plural rather than to a singular. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, just on that question of Gacanovic, and again not to belabour the point, but I think the issue there is if the Prosecution wish to rely on such a name -- I don't think I'll continue in view of the fact that the witness has just come into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it something --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In essence, Your Honour, the point is, and I can make this point in front of the witness, it is for the Prosecution to prove uniqueness as opposed to -- that's the point, Your Honour. And that's as far as I can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, uniqueness is not always proved through one singular witness, but is very often a combination of various elements, and not all these elements all necessarily have to prove the uniqueness of the situation. But altogether, taken altogether, it can give rise to another assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed. And thank you for your patience, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, before we go further with this conversation --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this moment, Your Honour, I'd like to ask the interpreters, with respect to the mention of the name Gacanovic that appears on -- in the B/C/S version of the transcript, page 5, that being the page with the ERN number 03220658, are they referring to Gacanovic in the singular or in the plural?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the reference to Gacanovici means plural, denoting a family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what we could hear on the tape. Because that's, of course -- let me just read it. I see that in the B/C/S version, it says Gacanovici. Is it a possibility, and I'm asking this first of all to the interpreters that Gacanovici would refer to a place rather than to persons? Because I noticed that many small villages where people of a certain name live, that the village or the place is given the same name, but then -- for example, I do understand that, for example, in a place called Ahmici, people with the name Ahmic might live there. I'm asking the interpreters, looking at the text on the page ERN last three digits 658, whether it is conceivable that reference is made by the word Gacanovici to a place rather than to persons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: Your Honour, it is indeed, in theory, possible according to the principle you've mentioned. It can only be established from the list of Bosnian place names, which exists, is available. Furthermore, this sentence itself is rather incoherent because the words that follow are "of course you know what's going on there." It is not clear whether it's a reference to a family or a place. Generally, it's an incoherent sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what raised my question, as a matter of fact, the word "there." Ms. Edgerton, we have established, at least if it's a correct transcript of the original B/C/S, that the word Gacanovici is used, which could refer to a plural of persons or to a place, if a place with this name exists. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, in this conversation, page 5 of the version you have before you with the page number 03220658, there's mention of the name Gacanovici. Do you see that portion I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a family in Ahatovici area by the name Gacanovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How common was that family name in Ahatovici settlement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the three large families inhabiting Ahatovici who practically founded the village of Ahatovici. Gacanovici, Mujkici, and the Novalijas. As for the place, there is no place called the Gacanovici. It's not the name of a village or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any individuals with the surname Gacanovic who were detained in the cistern with you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number. Many of them had died, in fact, were killed on the bus. A certain number were exchanged on the 13th of June in the former locality of Vogosca petrol station, but a large number of the Gacanovicis were killed in the massacre in Sokolje near Srednje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the incident you referred to yesterday in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to the massacre of the detainees from Rajlovac camp; more precisely, the small hangar of the Rajlovac camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you provide us with the name of any one of -- or a member of the Gacanovic family who was killed that you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Mujo Gacanovic, Mufid Gacanovic, Mustafa Gacanovic, Cazim Gacanovic, Alija Gacanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And with that, I think we can move on to the next and last --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before we move on, Your Honour, it might be clarified as to whether we're dealing -- this evidence here is evidence that is direct or indirect, if the witness is indicating this on the basis of direct observation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the names of those victims --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. The -- yes, the names of the victims and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, perhaps -- Ms. Loukas is seeking one clarification. When you just mentioned a few members of the Gacanovic family that died in the incident you referred to yesterday, did you observe these specific members of the family being there, or did you hear at any stage that they were among those who were on that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the persons I named, because I myself survived this massacre. Among those present were the people who were eventually killed, slaughtered, people whom I had known for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you because there were 50, so you might have observed some of them and heard about others at another moment. But you say the ones you mentioned, you saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I assert with absolute certainty that those persons were killed on the bus. On the footage on that tape, you can see the images of some of those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have one additional question for you. That's the following: The name Gacanovic, you told us it was one of the large families of your village. Do you know how common that name is outside your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a large number of the Gacanovicis living in a neighbouring place, Dobrosevici, with a total of 20 or so family houses occupied by people with that surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please correct me if I'm wrong, Dobrosevici is - but please correct if I am wrong - quite close to Ahatovici? It's the next village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, let's say if you're at a distance of 20 kilometres or 50 kilometres, do you know whether there were similar concentrations of the name Gacanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know, but I believe that this in this text the reference is particularly to those people from Ahatovici or Dobrosevici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you do not know about the -- how widespread the name is in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can move on to the next and last intercept, dated 15 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Unidentified female: Hello. Unidentified male: Yes? Unidentified female: Good evening. Can I speak to Mirko. Unidentified male: Mirko? Unidentified female: ... President Krajisnik's office. Unidentified male: Of course, just a minute. Unidentified female: Hello. Mirko Krajisnik: Yes. Unidentified female: Good evening, Mirko. Mirko Krajisnik: Good evening. Unidentified female: How are you? Mirko Krajisnik: I'm all right. And you? Unidentified female: Are you hanging in there? Mirko Krajisnik: Well, some shooting started. Unidentified female: Really? Mirko Krajisnik: Really. Unidentified female: Oh, please don't say that. Here, the president would like to talk to you. Mirko Krajisnik: Put him on. Momcilo Krajisnik: Hello. Mirko Krajisnik: Hello, Milan. Momcilo Krajisnik: What's going on? Mirko Krajisnik: Well, a lot of things. And how about you? Momcilo Krajisnik: My mate Momo is here, so I thought I'd ask you if you needed him to do anything for you. Nothing? Mirko Krajisnik: Nothing. I don't know what would be worth doing. Momcilo Krajisnik: What's going on? Mirko Krajisnik: I don't know what to tell you. Some shooting started right now. Momcilo Krajisnik: Where? Mirko Krajisnik: Cannons around the village. Momcilo Krajisnik: Around the village? Mirko Krajisnik: Yeah. Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, what is it? Are you being shelled or... Mirko Krajisnik: We're just trying to find out. It's dark, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Mm-hmm. Mirko Krajisnik: Did they inform you about that thing with Karkin? Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Mirko Krajisnik: And? Momcilo Krajisnik: We called the Presidency, but he had gone. I don't even know where. Mirko Krajisnik: 663-488. Momcilo Krajisnik: He called. Milena called him. Mirko Krajisnik: Stojko? Momcilo Krajisnik: Mm-hmm. Mirko Krajisnik: All right. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah, let me see. Mirko Krajisnik: Does he know how to leave a message or...? Momcilo Krajisnik: What did he tell you wanted? Mirko Krajisnik: He asked, did this guy bring you the message? Momcilo Krajisnik: What? Mirko Krajisnik: Has Milan been to see you? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, yeah, but forget that, man, I know he only called me because I had called. This is just about deception, you understand? Mirko Krajisnik: Yeah. Momcilo Krajisnik: He called me from Izetbegovic's office to check, but in front. Mirko Krajisnik: Where did he inform... ? He asked that you shouldn't shoot at the Yugoslav Airlines skyscraper up there. His mother has been wounded and things like that. Momcilo Krajisnik: Not to shoot at the Yugoslav Airlines skyscraper? Mirko Krajisnik: Yeah. Momcilo Krajisnik: Damn. Mirko Krajisnik: Listen. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes? Mirko Krajisnik: Vito called me. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah? Mirko Krajisnik: He's been up there today. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah? Mirko Krajisnik: So he wanted me to tell you the details and things like that. Momcilo Krajisnik: Has Simovic accepted this? Mirko Krajisnik: Yes, but he says it's a failure. Momcilo Krajisnik: Why? Mirko Krajisnik: He says this government is no good. He also told me there was a terrible fight at the Presidency session today. Momcilo Krajisnik: Why? Mirko Krajisnik: He said it really got ugly. Alija wants either Pusina or the public transportation company Gras director in the position of minister of internal affairs, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah? Mirko Krajisnik: And the guy from Kladusa wants this Delimustafic in that position, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Mirko Krajisnik: So they offered Delimustafic a position in reserves of supplies or something like that. Then he said, 'Wait, Alija, I'm not here to work for you. I'm a rich man. I'm not interested in money. I've supplied more goods in this war than any of you. So don't behave like that. You're obviously installing this Sandzak line, this guy from Sandzak in the Gras.' Then he said, 'It's easy for you to sit here in easy chairs eating lamb while people are there.' He told him all kinds of things, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Did Simovic really accept this, though? Mirko Krajisnik: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: He accepted? Mirko Krajisnik: Yeah, but when this guy told him it was a shame of him to have done so, that it was a puppet government dominated by Muslims in which Serbs played only a minor part, he allegedly said the government would fail because it wasn't set up properly. Momcilo Krajisnik: And Nikolic, too, right? Mirko Krajisnik: Did you see that? Ranko Nikolic? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, I can believe he had the guts to do this. Mirko Krajisnik: Well, they've done it. Their names had been published. Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, no, but I mean did they accept this or what? Mirko Krajisnik: Well, fuck, I don't know. On the whole, their names have been were published. They wouldn't have published their names if they hadn't accepted. Momcilo Krajisnik: Nah, that's just their proposal. Mirko Krajisnik: Then this guy said today that things aren't really functioning in the Presidency. Kecmanovic said all kinds of things, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah. Mirko Krajisnik: That people think the Serbs would get the Presidency because Alija can't get a third mandate. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah. Mirko Krajisnik: So he says you're thinking of becoming the Presidency Chairman, getting yourself a good deal, then some position as an ambassador. Reportedly the reformists have asked for Kecmanovic's removal. Momcilo Krajisnik: Why? Mirko Krajisnik: Well, he's not following the party guidelines, which put him in the Presidency. So they made the decision on Jure Pelivan without consensus and all kinds of things like that. Momcilo Krajisnik: What about Jure Pelivan? Mirko Krajisnik: The decision to appoint him prime minister. Momcilo Krajisnik: Mm-hmm. Mirko Krajisnik: No consensus was reached, you know. He said he had attached Pejanovic. He gave me a phone number in case you want to see him. Momcilo Krajisnik: Him? Mirko Krajisnik: Yeah? Momcilo Krajisnik: All right, give it to me. Mirko Krajisnik: He's got all kinds of things to tell. 619 494. Momcilo Krajisnik: What was that again? Mirko Krajisnik: 619 494. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right. Mirko Krajisnik: He says hello. It wouldn't be a mistake to call him, you know. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay, but what is he doing there? Mirko Krajisnik: He spent the whole day there after they had invited him. He was like, 'You will not drag me into this dirty business. You ignore Serbs everywhere.' He said all kinds of things. You'll hear it. Give him a call. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right. Mirko Krajisnik: What's going on up there? Momcilo Krajisnik: We've been really busy all day. Mirko Krajisnik: Screw it. This morning I heard that the Muslims who were running away from Misoca killed a bus full of Serbs in Srednje. Misoca was being cleansed. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes? Mirko Krajisnik: Some Muslims killed a full bus of Serbs. Momcilo Krajisnik: How? Mirko Krajisnik: They were on their way to Pale as refugees. Just a little while ago they told me this wasn't the case, but that in fact, they took these prisoners with them. Actually, an older sergeant who does exchanges up there received a phone call from the city. Can you hear me? Momcilo Krajisnik: Say again? Mirko Krajisnik: This guy from the city called him, you know. But what's his name, Alispahic, and he said those prisoners had been killed. Momcilo Krajisnik: What prisoners? Mirko Krajisnik: They took the prisoners to Pale again. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes? Mirko Krajisnik: At Srednje, they were intercepted by Muslims who killed all these prisoners. Our two men have been heavily wounded. Momcilo Krajisnik: They thought these were our people? Mirko Krajisnik: They thought those were our people. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Mirko Krajisnik: Tonight they want to retaliate against all Serbs in the city and in prison. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes? Mirko Krajisnik: To kill them all. Momcilo Krajisnik: Unbelievable. Mirko Krajisnik: Supposedly, they will use their cutthroats to attack Rajlovac in groups and all kinds of things like that. Momcilo Krajisnik: Unbelievable. Mirko Krajisnik: In retaliation. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right. I'll talk to you later. Tell our people there I said hello. Mirko Krajisnik: All right. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay. Just tell me one thing, who sent that girl there? I just don't get that. Mirko Krajisnik: All right, she is going tomorrow at 1100 hours. Momcilo Krajisnik: Going where? Mirko Krajisnik: To Belgrade. Momcilo Krajisnik: Oh really? Mirko Krajisnik: Mm-hmm. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right then. Mirko Krajisnik: Yes, well, um. These people didn't come, right? Momcilo Krajisnik: Who? Mirko Krajisnik: The two you talked about. Momcilo Krajisnik: Which ones? Oh, no, they will come. Today. We'll do something about that tomorrow. Mirko Krajisnik: We should do something about this thing here. Fuck, insinuations and these things are possible, too. Momcilo Krajisnik: All right. I'll talk to you later. Mirko Krajisnik: Just give it some thought. Check with kum Momo about that thing he was supposed to do for Zarko, please. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes, I've told him and I've given him instructions on this. Mirko Krajisnik: Right. Momcilo Krajisnik: Deal. Mirko Krajisnik: Deal. Call me before you go to bed. I'll be here. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah, we'll hang out here a little longer, and I'll call you before I go to bed. Mirko Krajisnik: All right. Bye. Momcilo Krajisnik: Bye.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that intercept having been concluded, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's just about the intercept, I don't know how many questions you would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would think no more than five, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could try to finish the intercepts, and then have a break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, in your testimony yesterday and this morning, you've told us that you were in a bus load of Muslims which was attacked at a location called Srednje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on that, are you able to -- could you tell us who they're referring to in this conversation when they say "at Srednje, they were intercepted by Muslims who killed all those prisoners. Our two men have been heavily wounded"?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obviously a reference to the massacre that happened in Sokolje near Srednje, in the vicinity of Ilijas. It's a reference to us, except that some nebulous things are stated here, like "Muslims were the ones who killed us" although the killers were Chetniks. This is ludicrous, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just moving somewhat earlier in the conversation to page 5 of the English language transcript, at the bottom, and I'll try and find the page in your transcript. The page with the number at the top right-hand corner 03220737, there's reference to an individual by the name of Alispahic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a family by the surname of Alispahic from the Ahatovici area?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a family with the surname Alispahic living in Ahatovici where they had a family house. His name was Bakid Alispahic. And at the time, he was in the centre of the security services of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Jahic, do you have any comment on this version of the incident that it was Muslims who mistakenly killed their own people on a bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be -- let's call it the methodology of how information was put out throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were stories going about to the effect that the Muslims were killing themselves, such as the Markale marketplace massacre and the one in front of the assembly. They said that the Muslims had thrown a grenade. So this is absolutely untrue because the people who followed us from Rajlovac, the Chetniks and our executioners, committed a horrendous crime in killing the 48 unarmed people at the Sokolje/Srednje place. And I personally saw the escorts following us from Rajlovac. And when the man returned and shot again at the dismembered bodies of the people there, he was the same man who had escorted us from Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think this man and the other members of the escort and your guards were Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say they were Serbs. They were Chetniks because there are decent Serbs, Orthodox Serbs in Sarajevo, but the people that did these things to us were brutal people. So I call them Chetniks. They were bestial, and they were the people who followed us from Rajlovac, escorted us from Rajlovac. And that's absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any factors that you could identify for the Court that would make you think they were something other than Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, there were four cars, and I mentioned them in my statement, the four cars that escorted us and followed us to that locality in Sokolje. And nobody could have known about us anyway because from the Vogosca/Sokolje junction we had to lie down. So if anybody was passing by, they would see -- they wouldn't see us. And then in the area where the massacre took place at that particular time, there was no fighting between the Muslims and Serbs going on during that particular period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes my questions about the intercepts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Edgerton. I would have one additional question to you. And that is the following, Mr. Jahic: One of the interlocutors says "Misoca was being cleansed." Could you tell us, Misoca, is that a village or a place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a place which comes within the frameworks of the Ilijas Municipality, I think, or not far from Ilijas anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know under whose control that village was during the war and whether there were any changes in control over that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say with any certainty at that point in time under whose control it was, the village of Misoca was, and whether that changed later on. I don't really know. I'm not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And during the -- well, let's say, during most of the time of the conflict, do you know in what area controlled by what party that village was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Misoca or the village where the massacre took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Misoca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Misoca. I really don't know. I can't say. So I don't want to say something I don't know about. Or whether that was it, because it was the beginning of the war, I don't know whether there was any fighting during that time there. I can't be certain, so I can't say because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, you can't tell us. We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour does that, of course Your Honour's aware that -- the witness can be excused, and I'll just make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you already escort Mr. Jahic out of the courtroom. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. As Your Honours are aware, Ms. Cmeric is not here. I've made certain arrangements to ensure that I can communicate with Mr. Krajisnik during the break. Of course, that means, Your Honour, we had an attempted communication prior to Your Honours coming on to the Bench. So there's a matter that we need to discuss. But the only issue is that I think if we come back at 11.00, that's not going to give us enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would have thought, say if we're 20 to 11 now, 10 past 11.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10 past 11.00. We'll adjourn until 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to the position during the break, the Registry have, of course, been very helpful in terms of attempting to assist the Defence with interpreters while Ms. Cmeric is away, which we're very grateful for, of course. There was a little delay because the particular translator they had on standby was in fact in another building. But we managed to conduct the conference. But there are always going to be, I think, administrative glitches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm glad that this problem has been resolved, and even the logistics of translators. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Jahic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I know you've asked a question about Misoca, and that was a village in which an exhibit was entered through Mr. Kljuc regarding the -- that was the Exhibit 299, which had some information on the ethnicity of that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you'll forgive me that it did not immediately come into my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, in an earlier meeting some time ago with an ICTY representative, did you provide that person with a copy of a videotape which relates to the events we have spoken about yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did the tape come to be in your possession?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came by the tape through a man who made the videocassette. He gave it to me personally. So the person who filmed it, that's where I got that whole videocassette from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you that he had filmed it?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I would say I've had it for quite some years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You viewed this video in its entirety on previous occasions, have you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right now, Mr. Jahic, I'm not going to play the whole video today, but in the interests of time I'm going to play you some clips, some shorter and some longer ones, from this video, and ask you to comment on what you see. There's -- we'll begin with two very short clips, each of several seconds. And they'll appear on the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I should ask Madam Registrar for an exhibit number for the transcripts. And of course the video itself.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video is P370, and the transcripts P370A and P370A.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the first clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving anything on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- Madam Usher, perhaps it should be replayed. And is the monitor of the witness on video or is it... Could the first clip be replayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on "computer evidence." Could it be replayed again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the second clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, did you recognise -- were you able to recognise what was depicted on the videoscreen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the bus in which the massacred bodies of the people from Ahatovici were still located. And the bus is on the road leading to Pale. And there's a stream, a brook there, that I described in my statement. And you can see the traces of blood oozing, dripping down the body of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your recollection, then, Mr. Jahic, does that -- do the videoclips that you've seen in the last few seconds of the bus look like the bus as it appeared to you after the incident you've described in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could -- we'll move on to the next segment, which is just under approximately five minutes long. And because this next segment is rather gruesome, I'm going to play through it without pause, and then I'm going to ask you a couple of brief questions at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] This one's just arrived as well. A bit more in reverse. Just to leave. It cannot be extended. Dig out down there. We will cover it. What is it? Put one on top of the other. Look, it's no good.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the third clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, do you recognise any of the persons depicted in this third videoclip?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, it's a horrendous massacre showing dismembered bodies, bodies without heads, parts of bodies missing. But despite all that, I have managed to recognise at least 60 per cent of the people shown on this footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of some of the individuals that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew my school friend. He went to eight years of primary school with me. His name is Zijad Mujkic. I also recognised another individual whom I spoke to, Mujkic Armin. And another one, Gacanovic, Mufid. I have stated his name already in my statement. Then next I recognised Ado Suljic, a person on the footage. Mirsad Mujkic was another one. Mehemed Mujkic, nicknamed Memo. And a person called Mesanovic. Nihad Mesanovic who was shoulder-to-shoulder with me. He was very close to me, and you can see him on the footage. The left-hand side of his head has been -- is missing. Blown off. And then some of the other people as well shown on the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps now we can move on to the last clip, which is about 7 minutes long. And I will pause at one or two occasions in the clip to ask you some very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's no sound coming from this clip, and it should have some.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] A sacred day such as St. Antony's day. In any case, let's continue with the news. The exchange of prisoners was carried in Rajlovac today. You've already heard that 37 people did not want to join the aggressor and that they remained in Sarajevo. But when you say aggressor -- however, one who is able to kill entire towns by shells or snipers is also able to treat the children, their mothers, and elderly people as prisoners. Take a look at the reportage of Mladen Vasiljevic. Significant exchange of prisoners took place in Rajlovac today. We're in this hall, where the only feelings are sorrow and misery. How many prisoners were handed over to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina? 391 prisoners were handed over to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They're mainly women, children, the sick, and the frail. We don't know. They were held in Rajlovac for 12 or so days, premises there and other premises, too. We don't know which ones. And the population from the Muslim villages of Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, yes, that's it Ahatovici and Dobrosevici were Muslim villages. We still don't know anything about the soldiers, who they are, middle-aged guys. We still don't know where they are and what happened to them as the women told us. And who did the Territorial Defence hand over to the Serb Territorial Defence to be exchanged. I don't know exactly how many people were handed over. There were the Chetniks, but I don't know who and how many. The women and children, I don't know exactly the number. In what condition are these people and who were imprisoned? Well, they were harassed, very exhausted, they were thirsty. They were undernourished. We took some women and children straight to hospital. They're all helpless, exhausted, and miserable. A little boy just got killed beside me. That is all that I can tell you. We were in the house, in the shelter. And they constantly shelled us. There were shells, shells, shells. They killed the cattle and the sheep and everything. They destroyed the houses. Everything. Did they burn them down? And who captured you? Who came to get you? I don't know. Some guys from up there. The Yugoslav Army. They had insignia of the Yugoslav Army. We surrendered to them. We were shelled for 19 hours, and then 5.000 shells were dropped. 280 were dropped in only two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if I can just pause the video at this point and ask you, Mr. Jahic do you recognise anyone depicted in the clip as you've seen thus far?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 90 per cent of the people that I saw I know because they're my neighbours. If you need their names and surnames, I can give them to you and tell you something about their fate, their fathers, who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "neighbours" do you mean people from the settlement of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among this group of people, did you have any close family members?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, all the people in Ahatovici are closer or more distant relatives. But as for my immediate family, it was my brother, father, my brother's wife, and their one-year-old baby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this young boy who's presently in the still --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this young boy whose picture you see in the still in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's his name?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Adnan Suljic, a boy who could have been 13 or 14 at the time. His father was killed on the bus. Later, he got killed himself as a result of the Chetnik shelling of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll just continue to the end of this clip now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I didn't. My father did. We were together in the shelter. They had white bands on their arms. They found us in the shelter, and they took us prisoners. They told us to come out and go with them. They took my husband from the cellar immediately. I don't know anything about my son. Everything that we had was burned down. I had an old house, car. Everything. Did you know some of those people? Yes, they were all our neighbours. They were laughing at us and waving to us while we were crying. Our children were crying. Of course, we recognised them. Our neighbours came to see us off. They gave children a small something while she was crying for her father. There she is. She hadn't seem him for seven days. We were there for 13 days. They were leaving, and the children were crying for them. They took them away and God only knows where. They put him in refrigerator plants. Look at her. She is hungry and thirsty. I don't have anywhere to return. I said so. There's no returning there. When our neighbours who were working in utility services and when it was necessary to clear the snow, he helped everyone, my husband did. He went also to places that nobody could reach. He would clear everything for them and look at what they've done to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That being the end of this last clip, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Jahic, do you recognise this last woman who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's her name?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fatija Muharemovic. This woman was also killed as a result of the Chetnik shelling of the city of Sarajevo, and the father of those two crying children is one of the persons we had seen in the previous film. The body in the red jumper with the head blown off. Those children were orphaned, and they are living with their grandmother who is seriously ill.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer. He seems to have said "got sick" or "fell ill."
