utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there are many such children who were orphaned with their fathers killed on that bus, and what we have just seen is an obvious example of ethnic cleansing wherein all the Muslim population was expelled from Ahatovici. The mosque in Ahatovici was blown up. And even some people from mixed marriages, Muslims and Serbs or Muslims and Croats were expelled. They participated in this exchange. They wanted an ethnically pure Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that concludes the Prosecution's examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Jahic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas who is counsel for the Defence, unless you would say that you need a short break at this very moment, then we would grant you a break. If, however, you say we can start with the cross-examination, Ms. Loukas will be invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I need a break, I will say so, because the films we have seen are very moving. I'm fine so far. But if I need a break, I'll tell the Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, I just want to echo what His Honour has indicated to you, and that is that if at any time you feel you need a break, please let me know. Now, obviously you have been through some events, some horrifying events that no human being should have to experience. So I will try not to touch too directly on the events. But if you find at any point that you need a break, please just let me know. Now, firstly, Mr. Jahic, I think you've given something in the nature of round about six statements to investigators from the ICTY and the Bosnian authorities in relation to the matters of which you've given evidence today and yesterday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's your 1993 statement to the Bosnian authorities, firstly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was a statement that I gave to the Bosnian authorities. It was rather the author of the book on the crimes in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm just dealing first of all with a statement taken by Ibrahim Pasic, Professor Ibrahim Pasic in 1993. That's your first statement in relation to the events. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do you say Ibrahim Pasic is?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may. It's not the first statement if you take into account the video film which also contains my statement, the first one I gave after I was saved from the bus, if you can call it a statement, what I said just after getting off that bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Jahic. I'm just here dealing with your written statements. So the first one is in time is, of course, 1993, which you gave to Professor Ibrahim Pasic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ibrahim Pasic is who?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a gentleman who was very interested, anxious to learn about the suffering of one people on the outskirts of Sarajevo. He wanted to write a book for these events to be recorded for future generations so that they can learn what happened there. So on the basis of some statements, he wrote a book about the crimes committed in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, of course, you gave a statement to investigators from the Tribunal in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1998, you gave a statement to the Bosnian Investigation and Documentation Agency. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a further information sheet to the International Criminal Tribunal in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a further correction statement in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a statement that you gave in 2002 in Sarajevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those six statements represent the written statements that you've given in relation to the matters you've given evidence of yesterday and today. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you gave evidence for the benefit of the Court and counsel at page 51, and I think it was touched upon earlier today as well. You indicated that -- you were asked this question by Ms. Edgerton: "Mr. Jahic, you said that one of the other detainees recognised this individual," referring to this person who threw some sort of device through the netted fence. And who was it that recognised this individual? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recognise the incident that I'm talking about there. Now -- and your answer was: "It was a friend of mine, a very close friend of mine and a former neighbour. He was a member of the reserve police force, and he recognised the said Chetnik as a former chauffeur and bodyguard for Krajisnik and Jovo Tintor. That Chetnik had arrived in an Audi." You remember that particular portion of your evidence yesterday. Correct, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. It was not a reserve member. It was a member of the reserve force of the regular police administration of Novi Grad. When you say "reservist," it could be misinterpreted. It is a member of the reserve force of the police administration of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Jahic. But what I'm reading to you is the translation that's come through. So I don't know if there was perhaps a mistranslation of what you had to say yesterday. But in essence, you agree with the fact that what you've said there is that he recognised the said Chetnik as a former chauffeur and bodyguard for Krajisnik and Jovo Tintor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that, I think Ms. Edgerton asked you some further questions today, and she asked you if you could remember the name of that person. The name of the person that was -- that had thrown this device in. And you said you couldn't remember at this time. If I take you to the 2002 statement that you gave that I referred to earlier, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and counsel, that's page 3 of the 2002 interview, just towards the bottom there, you refer to "on 12th of June 1992, a person nicknamed Zuti came by the vehicle Audi of red colour in front of the cistern. Detainee Armin Mujkic knew him personally. On that occasion Zuti threw a gas bomb inside the cistern." Does that assist you with your recollection, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you have finished with your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Does that assist you with your recollection? It does, does it?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment, it has to be clear to all of us that from that time, from the 14th of June 1992, 12 years have elapsed so that I may no longer remember some details that I remembered just after the fact. Maybe my memory has been refreshed through this. Maybe, after all, his nickname wasn't Zuti. Zuti wasn't a name in the former Yugoslavia. Zuti is a nickname. At least I don't know of anyone whose name is Zuti. It could only have been a nickname. As for the rest of the statement, it is evident, self-evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. So my question is that to your recollection, the person that Armin Mujkic had told you about was a person who had the nickname Zuti? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably true. I mean, Armin Mujkic recognised that person, I repeat, as the chauffeur and a man close to Krajisnik and Jovo Tintor because he, as a member of the reserve unit of the police administration of Novi Grad, worked for a while as part of the security detail guarding the house of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, just in relation to that, this information that you received from Mr. Mujkic, you realise, of course, that things you hear from other people might not necessarily be true. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But in this case, seeing how the person we're talking about is dead, it could be seen as a fact useful for elucidating this case of genocide, ethnic cleansing, a massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, I understand that feelings are running high and that you've experienced a lot. But you also appreciate that I have questions to ask you, and I need responses to my questions rather than references to --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Jahic, Mr. Krajisnik's driver is -- who was his driver? It is obviously a question of which you can give the Court no direct evidence. Correct? But before we go to that, you understand the difference between direct evidence and something you hear from someone else. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the question of who was Mr. Krajisnik's driver is obviously a question on which you can give the Court no direct evidence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if you take into account the fact that some photographs of these people are available, I could identify that person because I saw the person with my own eyes. What I heard from someone else is indirect, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, describe that person.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a person that arrived in an Audi, as I said. He was extremely stocky, a very large man. I would put his height at between 190 and 195, built as an athlete, fair-haired. He had cowlicks or maybe a receding hairline. I don't know. Maybe he was getting bald. Anyway, on that day, he came just outside the hangar and threw in that gas bomb with the intention of killing us, saying "don't be afraid, balijas. It's not a real bomb. Fuck your mothers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, may I just interrupt for one moment. Do you speak or understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not much. Could you please take your headphones off for one second. Ms. Edgerton, my question would be whether any formal position, what is the position of the Prosecution in respect of that formal quality of someone who came to that place? Because we see that -- of course the Defence responds to it. Is it -- what relevance does it have? I mean... Is there any suggestion that he might have communicated that to the person who employed him before?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One small factor that might go to show knowledge on the part of the accused, Your Honour, and together with that would be reference to the fact that the accused did live so close to the events where this was taking place. No more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So since he was formerly employed and since he was living nearby, that you would not exclude that a former employee might have met. Is there any further evidence for that, or is it just that -- the possibility which is not excluded?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The possibility which is not excluded, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, perhaps you can keep this in the back of your mind. If we -- I mean, who would exclude such a possibility? But no further evidence will be presented on that, and you'll understand that this may have its impact on the assessment of the importance and the relevance of this specific aspect of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I take on board what Your Honour has said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- and I have further question in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you assist the witness to put his headphones on again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, if I were to indicate to you that Mr. Krajisnik's driver was a man called Djuro Tadic who certainly does not have a nickname of Zuti and does not meet your description, you would know of nothing to directly contradict that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say and your knowledge. I say and state, and I have taken the solemn oath here to tell the truth and only the truth. Perhaps you do have that knowledge and information. I have told you what I have come here for; that is, to tell you everything about the case I know that took place during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Jahic. Now, moving on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, just for the Chamber to better understand both the testimony and your question, is there any time frame attached to what you put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik had the same driver before, during, and after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us any indication about already for how long? I mean, even before the war, if you have a driver -- well, let's say it could have been in 1991, and if someone then turns up, you could say, this is the former, and that could relate to 1989 or whatever. Could you give us a bit more indication on what the basis of your position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily at this very moment. If you say "I'll try to..."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's a problem, Your Honour, of not having Ms. Cmeric because I cannot communicate directly with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we could do, perhaps, is that the name you just mentioned -- I'm not the one of course who should guide the Defence, but if Mr. Krajisnik would write down the first day of the employment of the driver whose name you just gave, then it might assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. We'll revert to handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, handwriting is obviously very useful, Your Honour, and I can indicate we're covering a period here from the first day that Mr. Krajisnik was in parliament until he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Yes. What was just put to you by. Loukas, Mr. Jahic, covered the period on from the moment that Mr. Krajisnik was in parliament. I take it that this doesn't change in any way your answer where you said "I came here to testify of what I know," and I do understand that you heard that the man who appeared was a former driver and bodyguard of Mr. Krajisnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard -- let me repeat once again, that it was a man, first and foremost, who was close. Now whether somebody from the bodyguards or driver, if there was one driver, well, I don't know whether that is him or not. I can't know that, and neither can you. Now, whether there was anybody from his personal guard, personal bodyguard who would correspond to that description, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be sufficient, Ms. Loukas, for you to go to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would have thought so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, just going to your statement to the ICTY investigators in 1997, you, of course, told the truth in that statement, subject to corrections that you later gave in 2000 and 2001. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As, in fact, you've told the truth in all your statements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 5 of your ICTY statement, in English it's the third paragraph for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and counsel, and it's the first paragraph in the B/C/S version, you indicate there, and I'll just read it to you, there's no need to have the statement before you. "My earlier statement" - this is what you've got in your ICTY statement; I'm just about to read it to you. "My earlier statement from March 28 1993 mentions that Seseljovici and Arkanovici and other soldiers were attacking Ahatovici. The figure of 15.000 aggressor soldiers is likely correct, but there is no way I could have known who was attacking the village. I would like to make this clear from my earlier statement. I think the man who was transcribing the statement has inserted this." Do you recall that portion of your ICTY statement that I'm referring you to, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you want me to clarify some particulars related to the Seselj men and Arkan's man, Seseljovici and Arkanovici, I saw a lot of that Chetnik army, and that doesn't exclude the possibility of them being Seselj's and Arkan's men, but I can't say with any certainty. So, probably, that is the idea presented by the author compiling that text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you don't exclude the possibility, but what I want you to do is just -- because this will take a while if we're not focussed on you actually answering the question that I'm asking as opposed to adding other aspects in. And we're always subject to time limitations here. If you can answer a question with a yes or no answer, that would be very useful in terms of ensuring that we're focussed on what the questions are. You understand what I'm saying, of course?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand. However, there might not be answers that you can express with just a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to explain to you, Mr. Jahic. The question put to you by Ms. Loukas was just about whether you remembered that you made that statement, and then she would have some specific questions. If at the end of the questions put by Ms. Loukas you think that there is something very important missing, you could always address us. But Ms. Loukas might have specific points in mind which she would like to clarify. So if she first asks you whether you remember that statement, I think there a yes or no could do. And then let's first hear what specific questions she would have. And if at the end something should be added, please address me. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the situation there is, Mr. Jahic, that you think that the man who was transcribing your statement from 1993 has inserted the mention of Seseljovici, Arkanovici. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 6 of your ICTY statement, that's, for the benefit of counsel and the Trial Chamber, first paragraph in the English statement and last paragraph of page 5 in the B/C/S statement. Now, there you indicate that -- and you're dealing at the time there with the attack on your village. And you indicate there "one of the Chetniks had something like a Zolja pointed directly at us all this time. He fired it above our heads at a nearby Muslim house behind us. I know which house was hit and it burnt down. As regards this mention in my March 28, 1993, statement of the house having been the headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company, I think those are the words of the man who took my statement. This may have been such a headquarters, but I have never known any information to that effect." Now, you recall, of course, that portion of your ICTY statement in 1997, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your 1993 statement, you indicate that the statement [sic] that was burned down was the headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company. That was in your 1993 statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I mean, from 1993 to 1997, that's a four-year period. So perhaps my memory was fresher at the time about some of the events. As I say, it's been a long time since then, 12 years, in fact. But all the more important things, the essential points that are in the statement, are ones that I can remember. I remember the name of that person who fired from the Zolja, for instance. Now, at that point in time, perhaps I had more information and knew whether it was staff or not, headquarters or not. As far as I'm concerned, for me, those -- well, the Defence seems to be attaching itself to some minor points. That is their right, of course. But we must bear in mind the essentials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, may I ask you to refrain from commenting on the Defence position because matters that might be of great importance for the Defence, although are not in the centre of how you experienced this time, you might not be aware of the importance of that. So if you would please answer the questions put by Ms. Loukas, and we'll later have to assess what is important, most important for this case. And apart from the very emotional experiences you had, there might be other aspects that are also relevant for this Chamber to hear. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you do understand that it is the Judge's job to listen to the answers that you give from questions from both the Prosecution and the Defence. You appreciate that fact, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back to what I was asking you, the 1993 statement that you gave indicates that there was this house in your village which was the headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company. And you refer to that in your statement to the Tribunal. Correct? We're agreed up to this point, are we?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the case, that the -- that this house was the headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, perhaps in 1993, and that's quite logical, I had fresher recollections and I stated them at the time. Now, after all that time, I can't say with certainty whether the Chetnik hit the house, that house or another house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Jahic, that it was the headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company at the time.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you reformulate your question, please. Do you know that it was the headquarters? Is that what you're saying, or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what's said in your 1993 statement: "When we surrendered I saw with my own eyes when Marinko Simeutovic fired a grenade at a house in which -- during the attack on the village was located the headquarters of the 3rd Platoon of the Ahatovici Company. The house was set on fire immediately, and very soon it burned down." That's what's contained within your 1993 statement.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that was it. Because that's when I made the statement, so that must have been it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your 1997 statement to the Tribunal, you say that "as regards this mention in my March 1993 statement of the house being the headquarters of the 3rd platoon of the Ahatovici Company, I think those are the words of the man who took my statement. This may have been such a headquarters, but I have never known any information to that effect." And we agree that that's contained within your ICTY statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're asserting that that portion of what's contained in your 1993 statement was inserted by the man who took your statement, Mr. -- Professor Ibrahim Pasic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I said so then, but when you live through the kind of thing to live through, a genocide of that type, you can't remember some of the minor details. There were many statements. Now, whether there could have been a mistake, whether I actually said that, some of those minor, unimportant points I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In relation to your 1993 statement again, you state this: "During the Chetnik attack on the village of Ahatovici, as a soldier of the BH armed forces, I was fighting against the Chetniks, former JNA, Seselj, and Arkan's soldiers." That's part of your 1993 statement. Are we agreed?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I don't have the statement before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just going to make the suggestion that it might be helpful to either have a break at this time or provide the witness with a copy of his 1993 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I can't imagine that a witness to whom certain lines are read --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be discussed in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please take your headphones off, or perhaps we'll have a break. Perhaps That might be better. Mr. Jahic, we're going to have a break. Could you follow Madam Usher and leave the courtroom. We'll continue in approximately 20 or 25 minutes. Ms. Loukas, if it is asked to someone what he said some 11 years ago, he might not be certain about whether that was really exactly what he said or not, and therefore has had some hesitations to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have a written statement. I'm happy to put the written statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, to some extent, it's part of what I call the ritual questions, whether that's his statement. Of course that's his statement as it's written down unless there was any forgery in place which I do not expect to be there. So therefore, I think this Chamber would not mind, first of all, if you give his B/C/S version of the statement to the witness, and then -- unless there would be any objection from the Prosecution, that we just say, as you can see, you gave a statement saying that, and then put further questions to the witness, instead of just asking him to reread it all and ask whether this was his statement. Of course, if he could correct that statement, but he has done that already in many instances in later statements. I think it would be more practical to find a more direct way to confront the witness with any inconsistencies or uncertainties because that's what I understand you're doing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because of course the statement taken in 1993 was of course closer to the events. And of course, the matters that I've taken the witness to are not, in fact, minor discrepancies but matters of some significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not blaming you for going into that area, but a more direct way might be easier for the witness and would not -- if there's no objection from the Prosecution, the Chamber would allow you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The -- what time did Your Honour say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said 20 to 25 minutes, and I had in mind that we would need 2 or 3 minutes, and we will adjourn until a quarter to 1.00. But if there's anything you'd like to raise at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course, we have the interpreter on standby again. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you think you --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Because we didn't manage to finish the conference on the last occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, I do understand. On the other hand, I'm a bit concerned about -- the Defence asked for not sitting on Thursday and Friday, and we granted that. And yesterday you gave me a clear impression that we would finish with the two witnesses before Thursday. Is that still your expectation?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually no, Your Honour. I must say, in view of the fact that I received again by email last night a supplemental information sheet in relation to the next witness introducing new matters, Your Honour, that will require additional investigation. And in those circumstances, I think that we'll probably get through the evidence in chief. But, Your Honour, it's not a question of the Defence being able to cross-examine when it contains new material at the last moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we do not know what the exact impact is, but that would mean we should keep a witness here from Wednesday until next Monday. Mr. Hannis, do you have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we became aware of this possibility, we spoke with the witness and, Your Honour, I would rather if we could not finish his cross-examination this week, not have him stay over. This has been a very emotional time for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness, or this one? It's the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next witness. Something that came up in the proofing was very difficult for him, and I think it would be better if he were able to go home and come back in two weeks or something, rather than staying over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try very much to focus on what's the core of the case. This case as far as I understand should finally not depend on whether there is an opportunity, although further unproven, that someone who might have been employed before that he could have contacted. I mean, we are far off from what's the core of the case. I'm not blaming you, Ms. Loukas, because it has been introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I have to meet it. Once it has been introduced by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it also depends on the relevance and the importance. And what you also could, as I did before, say what's the importance for the Prosecution. I mean, you can't strike anything out, although you could even consider that, and say: Well, that's in his previous statement. But that would cause all kinds of deep investigations that might lead to nowhere. So therefore, whether we should just ignore the parties, we'll ignore that a person who came in an Audi was said to have earlier been employed which could lead to a possible conclusion that if you're employed by someone before, that you might have contacted him at a later stage. Of course, I could have contacted over the last two weeks my boss of 20 years ago. But it's not very likely, and it's really not the core of the case. So I'd like the parties to concentrate of what's really the important part. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just will make one comment in relation to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that is that, firstly, the Tribunal does accept hearsay, subject to weight, firstly. Secondly, Your Honour put a question to the Prosecution in relation to this evidence, and they said that they were relying on it. And it's incumbent on the Prosecution to focus their case so that the Defence can also focus their case. If the Prosecution proceeds in a sort of an - and I'm not blaming Ms. Edgerton for this - but, you know, sort of open-slather fashion, you know, every [inaudible] is part of the mosaic, then, Your Honour, we're forced to ensure that we cover every angle as well, when one is dealing with charges as serious as these and the wide notions of joint criminal enterprise and command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to refer to this very example, the weight that a reasonable Chamber could attach to this possibility in order to support a decision negative for Mr. Krajisnik is, and I think all parties would understand that, is if not zero, close to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that case, it shouldn't be introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I also urge the parties to see whether these kind of matters that take a lot of time and are not in the core of the case could not be avoided either by saying: Well, if you really would like to keep this or this element in, then we have to spend a lot of time on it. And I think it -- of course, I'm not -- I cannot forecast what the future will bring us. But I hardly can imagine that either the Prosecution or Defence would expect that this would really -- an element that was worth so much attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and this is the sort of material that shouldn't be introduced as part of the Prosecution case, full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. We observe that notion. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, were you a soldier of the Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Territorial Defence of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going on to your 1993 statement, and we have a copy of the B/C/S version of your 1993 statement that I can put before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I indicate to the Court that we produced some copies, but the Prosecution also helpfully provided some copies as well, Your Honour, which was gratefully received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have that statement before you, the B/C/S version of your 1993 statement, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to the last page of your statement. Have you got the last page of your statement, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look -- do you see paragraph 25 there where you have stated -- this is in reference to the bus. "The massacre was probably committed by people from our escort whom I saw when I boarded the bus. I do not know their names, but I may be able to recognise them." Do you see that portion of your statement there?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So of course, at the time you gave that statement, you indicated that the -- that you weren't sure that the -- it was committed by people from your escort. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certain, but as I stated in a supplement to this text, the author took the liberty. Later I made some corrections. I don't know which exactly, but as for my statement quoted here, I stated that I personally saw one man out of the escort shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, you've said nothing about that man in your 1993 statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which man?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you've just indicated in your last answer. "Personally saw one man out of the escort shooting."

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one with the Audi?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him personally shooting, and that Audi followed us from Rajlovac to the site of the massacre because I saw that car again come back to the scene of the crime and the man shoot at the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, I understand you say that now. But you agree with me that you say nothing about that man coming back and shooting in your 1993 statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it is not in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, these are the kind of ritual questions that, of course, the Chamber can read the statement and if it does not appear there, then it's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not a jury. Even without specifically drawing the attention -- if you say there's a difference as far as this man is concerned, because it doesn't appear in the 1993 statement, then, of course the Chamber is perfectly able to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Perhaps the witness might be able to remove his headphones for a minute while I address Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless it's really of great importance. I mean, you've put the questions that you go but it's just -- you always say "a marker," it's what a marker is for.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It is a marker. Indeed, Your Honour. Now -- I think that the witness might have to then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He took them off already. I didn't notice that. There was even no need, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic, for removing your microphones. But fortunately, there was no need after all. Now, just in relation to your use of the term "probably" in your 1993 statement, you say there that that is something is that Mr. Ibrahim Pasic inserted this your statement. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a number of things. As far as I can see, that statement was drawn up for the purposes of a book. It's not a statement drawn up by any official authorities or anything. He probably asked me things that interested him, although there are quite a few things here that have not been included in the statement. It's the statement that I gave for the purposes of this book, "Crimes in Ahatovici." It was not part of an investigative procedure or an interview where everything would be stated, asked and answered precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is, Mr. Jahic, that you can't be certain who committed that atrocity. That's the case, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain about the identity of those who committed the crime, and I even named the person from the escort who drove the vehicle that I also identified. I saw him shooting. I saw him throw two hand grenades into the bus, and I saw him leave in the direction of Srednje. I included that in my statement -- here in my testimony, rather, under solemn oath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, you didn't mention these matters to Mr. Pasic who took your 1993 statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you again that Mr. Pasic is a professor, a writer. He asked me about the things that interested him. I don't even know whether this statement can be used as evidence. There are some things in it that I didn't say, and on the other hand there are other things that happened that I knew for certain and that are not included in this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to your 1993 statement again, you refer to Sok interrogating you. Do you see that portion of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page? Can you tell me so that I can find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's page 3 in the English, and it's the paragraph that mentions Mr. Hasan Mujkic. That's paragraphs 15 and 16 in the B/C/S version. So it's page 2, and it's the third-last and second-last paragraphs. Now, you refer there to being interrogated by Sok, and him asking you about your role in the war, about mortars, about Hasan Mujkic, our commander, about snipers, et cetera. "I tried to convince him that the people who were responsible for mortars and snipers were not among the prisoners and that they had escaped towards Visoko." That's true --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so that portion, Dr. Pasic got correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we were to speak to Mr. Pasic, I take it he would confirm that all these matters that are contained within the statement are not matters that you told him; some are, some aren't. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that calls for some speculation on the part of the witness. I don't know how he could know what Mr. Pasic might or might not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I think that the witness -- whether it would be confirmed by Mr. Pasic or not is, of course, something the witness could not know, could he?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I'm happy to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, just going to your statement there in relation to Hasan Mujkic, he was, in fact, your local commander in the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the Territorial Defence of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to take you to your 1997 statement to the ICTY authorities. And we have a copy of that statement in B/C/S for you, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one question, if I may ask: Is it possible to use in these proceedings statements made by a person who is not competent to collect statements? He is a writer. He's not a member of the police, of the ICTY, of the agency for investigations and documentation or anything. I don't know to what extent this statement is authoritative or authentic. It's made by an author, a writer. I don't even know how this statement got here, how it ended up in the ICTY. Because this is a man who wrote books, and as an author he could have inserted his own ideas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jahic, the Chamber clearly understood your testimony that when you were confronted with this statement, that you expressed as your view that parts of it were words spoken not by you, and that you have drawn your attention to the special character of this statement, and this was not unobserved by the Chamber. To what extent it's used, it's not -- first of all, that statement is not in evidence apart from the parts that were read to you. And I think it's -- the Defence, perhaps also the Prosecution wants to get a clearer view on the consistency of your recollection over the years. And I think both parties have well understood that you say that the 1993 statement might not serve for that purpose very well since you are not convinced that everything what you said is reflected in it, just as some of what is said in that statement might not have been your words. So I think the parties noticed that; the Chamber certainly noticed that as well. And then we'll finally assess what the use could be. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I indicated, the B/C/S version of Mr. Jahic's ICTY statement should now be before him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jahic, if we go to what is page 4 of the English, the third paragraph, and in the B/C/S, page 4 of the second paragraph, which is paragraph 21 - I think that statement is numbered. I'll just wait until you get to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that's the paragraph that reads "we started to organise ourselves in connection with the Novi Grad TO staff. All together, there was between 120 and 150 of us. Our commander at that time was appointed by the Novi Grad TO. I don't know who it was. We used to go to buy weapons and get supplies from TO Visoko. A certain number of people were required for that trip to organise protection through Chetnik territory for the people who were carrying the weapons. I was part of that protection squad." So just in relation to that paragraph, how many times did you act as protection for obtaining weapons?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of weapons were obtained?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, as I said in my statement, it was light infantry weapons. Mainly semi-automatic and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of those were obtained?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you -- I'm not asking you to be precise. I'm asking you to be approximate.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a fact that could help us get to a specific answer to that question is that we were about 120 men. And if we know that not all of us had those rifles, some of us had makeshift weapons or self-made rifles. Maybe 70 per cent out of those 120 men had those light infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you got about 70 light infantry weapons from the Territorial Defence of Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, it was more than a couple?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it's approximately 85. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Approximately 85, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that, Mr. Jahic, you indicated in your evidence yesterday at page 13 that -- and of course you gave the Trial Chamber the truth yesterday when you were giving your evidence, as you are today. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've indicated today that you got about 70 light infantry weapons from the Territorial Defence of Visoko. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, could you please clearly answer the questions because the interpreters have difficulty in hearing you. We'll put the microphone a bit closer. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because yesterday you were asked at page 13, for the benefit of counsel and the Trial Chamber, "How did you get a hold of those weapons?" And your answer was: "Well, some people from Ahatovici had purchased their weapons, which was possible, just before things started happening. I don't know exactly where they bought them, but I know weapons could be bought up to a certain time. Some of the weapons came from the Territorial Defence of Visoko, but I stress again it was only a couple of rifles." So which one's the truth? What you're saying today, or what you gave evidence of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I just told you the percentage of weapons we obtained, maybe I gave too hasty an answer yesterday. You can determine by comparison. We had that many weapons, and it was a certain small portion of what the Chetniks had in their barracks, in their arsenals. So you can view it as some sort of comparison. Some people indeed bought rifles. But if you know that the total number of people who had those rifles was -- I don't remember what exactly was said, Your Honour, what number you gave. 70, I think. That also includes the number of rifles we received from the Territorial Defence. And just a minute, if you'll excuse me, Your Honour, before I continue, I would appreciate it if we could have better coordination of interpretation because it happened several times already that my words are being taken and placed into a different context. Once already I talked about the reserve police force, and it was interpreted as reservist. Another time, Zuti was referred to as a name, where it's actually a nickname. So maybe you should take into account, then, in the process of interpreting from the Bosnian language some things are placed in a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you observe that there's any translation problem or whenever you find that in view of a question that's put to you at a later stage that there could be a translation problem, please address me. Until now, I think we identified them. And our interpreters are doing a very difficult job, and they are doing it quite well. But whenever there's any shortcoming, please address me. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back to the evidence you gave yesterday, page 17 for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the Court, you gave some evidence about watching the attack from the Rajlovac barracks against the Sokolje-populated area with your own eyes. So you watched that from Ahatovici. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far in terms of kilometres is Ahatovici from the Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely, but I believe it's 4 to 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the -- from Ahatovici where you were watching, how far is the Sokolje populated area that you referred to in your evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, similarly, the populated area of Rajlovac and the populated area of Sokolje are only divided by a road that passes through. They are very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't, of course, have the benefit of binoculars, did you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure whether I was watching through binoculars or not, but the configuration of Ahatovici is such that its altitude is higher than that of the surrounding populated areas. So you could see well even without binoculars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that from a distance of 4 to 5 kilometres, that you were able to see the attack. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that -- as you indicated yesterday, that you believe that artillery weapons were used in that attack. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these attacks --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And infantry weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these attacks were mounted in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, since these attacks were numerous, they usually started in the evening and lasted into the night using infantry weapons with some sort of light-emitting rounds so that you could see exactly where they were headed. And the same goes for artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on to another topic, in your evidence yesterday at page 20, you indicated that on the 2nd of June 1992, our defence, the defence of the Ahatovici settlement could no longer resist the attacks launched by the Chetniks so that they managed to break through our defence lines at three or four places, and they started entering the Ahatovici settlement. Now, I think you indicated in your ICTY statement that there were about -- that you'd organised about between 120 to 150 of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 120 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this attack, of course, was -- went for a period of over five days, from about the 25th of May until the 2nd of June when there was surrender. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th. Not the 20th of May, but the 29th of May to the 2nd of June. Or rather to the fall of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're dealing then with a period of -- the 2nd of June would be the fifth day. Correct? We're dealing with a period of, say, four to five days. We'd be agreed on that, would we not?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also indicated in your statement that there were 1500 aggressor soldiers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a rough estimate of mine, taking into account the fact that around Ahatovici, there were three large military facilities, or rather three large barracks, Rajlovac, Butile, and Ilijas. And in view of the fact that Vogosca -- at Vogosca, there was a large concentration of Chetniks, or rather the aggressor army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So would it be right to say, then, that over a period of four to five days, 120 to 150 men were able to keep away 1500 soldiers? Is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at it this way, those attacks were artillery ones, heavy artillery was used. And the true intention was to kill as much of the population as possible, or rather the people who had taken part in the defence, to set fire to the area, to create an atmosphere and mood of war. There were one or two attempts, for example, on the part of the infantry during that time, but they kept shelling the area between the 29th of May until the 2nd of June 1992. And many houses were burnt down. Many people were wounded in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, were you aware of a plan by fighters from Ahatovici to attack the Butile military barracks?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say with certainty that there was no attack being prepared, nor was there any attack at all during the period from 1992 or in 1992. It would be unthinkable that 120 people would go against a barracks in Butile, which was a well-fortified feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in view of the time that we have available, Mr. Jahic, I'm going to put a number of questions to you that should hopefully be capable of a yes or no answer which would mean, I think, that we could finish this afternoon so that you don't have to stay an additional day in The Hague. And I think we can probably get through them in about 10 minutes. Okay, were you aware of Mr. Hasan Mujic being chief commander of a paramilitary formation in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a paramilitary formation. It was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But yes, he was the commander of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of soldiers from Ahatovici seeking to link Sarajevo and Visoko via Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of soldiers from Ahatovici seeking to link territorially Sarajevo and Visoko via Rajlovac? Were you aware of a plan of that nature?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no other soldiers, except the locals of Ahatovici, people who were residents there who had lived there since time immemorial, lived in Ahatovici. There were no other soldiers. As for a plan, I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of joint patrols being organised in and around April and May in Novi Grad Municipality, particularly in Dobrosevici? That is joint patrols of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no such patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of a -- checkpoints being set up by all three peoples, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats in your local municipality?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no checkpoints, except the barricades on the two bridges that I mentioned yesterday during my testimony. So they were barricades on the bridges at Reljevo and Bojnik through which we were not able to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could we just verify that there's no -- you said municipality, which would cover the whole of -- the whole of the municipality, or just the part where the witness lived? There might be some misunderstanding. When you said there were no checkpoints, would that be true for the whole of the municipality, or were you just describing what happened in the area close to where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Ahatovici specifically, because we couldn't know what was going on in Novi Grad, for example, because we weren't able to reach Novi Grad because of the barricades that had been erected on the two bridges that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas, that at least clarifies that the answer of the witness is limited to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of a meeting in your local area, in the area of your community and Dobrosevici, that there was a meeting in order to maintain and promote peace, and they invited people from all the populated areas in your local community in the second half of the month of April 1992? Are you aware of a meeting of that nature? The meeting was held in the cultural centre in Reljevo.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know something about the event. Some of our neighbours called us. And several times in different ways, they tried to bring us into certain places, probably to make their job easier, like they did in the other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you were not at that meeting. Is that correct, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't think the meeting ever actually took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I were to tell you that a meeting of that nature did take place, you would have no direct evidence to contradict that, would you, Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you my own personal opinion now. You can take it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jahic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Is there any need to put any further questions to the witness, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to ask you for a clarification, if I may. During your testimony yesterday, you described the attack against your village, Ahatovici, and you said that the women and the children and the elderly were -- had taken refuge in a building, in a building in the village, and that the attacking forces targeted that building, knowing full well that the building was inhabited or occupied by these women, children, and elderly persons. Now, how did you arrive at that conclusion, that the attackers knew who was in the building?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could see and target with their snipers in unimpeded fashion because the configuration of the terrain around Ahatovici is such that the surrounding hills and the houses inhabited by Bosnian Serbs were up in the hills, and Ahatovici is in the valley down below. So you had a good view of the whole of Ahatovici. It was like in the palm of your hand. And they were the Koprivica houses, Stepovac, the Krstac hill. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But that's your personal conclusion? You haven't got any concrete information about that? That's what you yourself deduce?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could see what was going on because it was very close by. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is they saw the women and children and elderly moving towards that particular building, that house, and they waited for them to get there, and then launched their attack on that house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, you could say that that is what happened. But while they were in the house itself, some of those women and the people there, the elderly people, had to go out of the shelter, leave the shelter. Because to be inside five days without any food or water, it was actually a cellar that they were, a dark cellar, so people had to go outside to get a breath of fresh air, for example. There were 150 people there, so when you have that many people in such a small space, 50 square metres or 70 square metres of dark space, they had to leave from time to time. And so I assume that they were noticed and that the people knew where the women and children were. They had seen them, happened to see them. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were attempts of that kind to target that house. But the house was -- the premises were more or less secure because there were three concrete levels. It's a three-storey house, so these three concrete layers protected the bullets from coming into the cellar, entering the cellar, which is where the people were, the civilians. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] All right. Now quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no interpretation of the last question that Mr. -- that Judge El Mahdi asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. I was just about to interfere. The last question you put to the witness has been answered, but the question as such has not been translated into English. I remember that the last words were "a votre avis." JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. My question was this: It had to do with the possibility of targeting people who were below ground by attacking the building itself, or rather something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the question has been answered. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, very quickly, please, during the bus incident, do you remember whether there was an exchange of gunfire at all? Not from the bus, but in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no firing, no exchange of gunfire or shooting around the bus, just the direct shots and shooting at the bus by the Chetniks. In that period of time and in the area where the massacre took place, there was no fighting. There wasn't a war going on. The Serbs and Muslims lived quietly there, and the road separated those two areas, the area inhabited by the Serbs and the area inhabited by the Muslims. So they weren't in conflict. There wasn't a situation of conflict. There was no shooting or fighting in that particular area. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But in your opinion, you had some notions of military matters and Territorial Defence, some things like that. In your opinion, wasn't there the possibility of shooting if the aim was to liquidate you?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation] JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Do you have an explanation why, why they targeted the bus and not the individuals? If you have no explanation for that, never mind.

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you put that question a different way, please. Can you ask it again. I'm not sure I understood it. I'm not sure I was able to follow your question. Could you repeat, please. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Well, the simplest thing would have been to have you step down from the bus, and then to liquidate you that way, to shoot you that way, once you were outside, if that was the object, to target you personally, rather than shooting at a bus, at a whole bus. Wouldn't that have been simpler?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand the question now. My personal opinion about all that is that we were not supposed to be liquidated at that particular spot because we were probably supposed to have been taken to Pale or Sokolac, and then executed there. And then there would have been no witnesses to come in here today and testify to the events that took place on the 14th of June 1992. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, I've only one very short question to you. Did you ever hear any information about two of the persons not belonging to your ethnicity being killed at that same event? Whether it would be those escorting the bus, as you told us, or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ELVIR JAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were escorts or of other -- from other ethnicities, they were not killed then. There were 48 killed persons from Ahatovici, and let me repeat under oath, having taken the solemn declaration and of sound mind, they were killed by people from the escort, the Chetniks that had brought them from Rajlovac, in fact. And I'm on the right road because some security services are on the right path to learning who the perpetrators were and learning their identity so that one day they, too, could be brought into this court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jahic, this concludes your testimony in this Court, unless one of the parties would have a need to put additional questions triggered by the questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, no questions triggered by Your Honours' questions on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Jahic. You've answered the questions put by both parties to you, and the questions put by the Bench. It did not remain unnoticed that you are taken back to events and experiences that must have been very emotional for you. The Chamber is grateful that you came, that you testified, and wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Jahic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any procedural issues at this moment? I do understand, I have to reread the transcript, Ms. Loukas. Was it your position that the supplemental information would not allow you to cross-examine the witness, or not even to start the cross-examination of the witness? I have to compare the original statement with the supplemental information sheet the Chamber received this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. My view is that the additional information requires further investigation, certainly not the sort of investigation, Your Honour, that can be conducted overnight firstly. Secondly, as I understand it, the evidence of this next witness is scheduled to take, I think, four hours, which would in any event take up all the time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's to be regretted that we could not finish this week with these two witnesses. I spent already enough time in addressing the parties in increasing the focus on the most important elements of the testimony. I'll not repeat that again, but I hope that the parties will keep that in the back of their mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say from my perspective, I do agree with the indication that Your Honour's given, but it does take two to tango.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I said I don't want to elaborate on it any more, except to say I thought the message was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the interpreters could still assist us, then we'll try to deal with the exhibits right away, and then adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

P369C and P369C.1, transcript of P369, 15 June 1992. P370, CD containing four videoclips. And P370A and P370A.1, transcripts of P370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are no objections, they are admitted into evidence with this addition: That P368, the short description should be black and white photocopy of a photograph of a person standing at the entrance of a hangar, which is the neutral description of what we can see on the photograph. I'd like to thank the interpreters again for their patience, and the same for the technicians. We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I, if I'm not mistaken. Yes, Courtroom I.
